ety.text: From Middle English vntil, until, untill, ontil, ontill, perhaps representing a northern variant of Middle English unto (see Modern English unto). By surface analysis, un- (“against; toward; up to”) + till.

senses.d: Up to the time of (something happening); pending.
ex: If you can wait until after my meeting with her, we'll talk then.
Keep walking until the second set of traffic lights, then turn left.
He rousd himselfe full blith, and hastned them untill.

senses.d: Up to the time that the foods or other things available to sell, or tasks which need to be completed, run out.
ex: Every Friday 2pm-until and Saturday 5pm-until[;] we are located inside the dollar general parking lot

senses.d: Up to the time that (a condition becomes true).
ex: Not until I got his email did I fully understand his disappointment.
It took us a week before/until we got the house repainted.

ety.text: Inherited from Old French jusque, from Latin inde + ūsque.

Inherited from Old Spanish fasta, and of ultimate uncertain origin. Commonly proposed etymologies are Arabic حَتَّى (ḥattā, “until”) and Latin ad ista (“to this”). pt:até.gl: until (up to the time of something happening)

ety.text: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese até, ata of uncertain origin. Possibly from Arabic حَتَّى (ḥattā), Latin ad ista (“to this”) or Latin ad tenus (“as far as”) (>"ad tenes"), which explain the large number of mediaeval variants (atrõe, atée, atrõo, attaa, atẽe, atães, tẽe and so on).
Inherited from Middle French avant, from Old French avant (“before, prior in time, forward”), from Late Latin ab ante (“before, in front of”), from Latin ab (“from”) + ante (“before”).

es:antes.gl: before (earlier than) (triggers the subjunctive in subordinate clauses)

ety.text: Inherited from Old Spanish antes, from ante with the adverbial -s, the former from Proto-Indo-European *h₂énti.

fr:jusqu'à ce que.gl: until (up to a given moment in time)

ety.text: Inherited from Middle English unto, from Old English *untō, *und tō, equivalent to un- (“against; toward; up to”) + to. Cognate with Old Frisian ont to ("until"; > Saterland Frisian antou (“until”)) (cf. Old Frisian und (“up to; till”), Old Frisian til (“till; to”)), Old Saxon untō, untuo (“until”), Old High German unze, unzi, unza (“until”), Old Norse und (“as far as; up to”), Gothic 𐌿𐌽𐍄𐌴 (untē, “until; as long as”).

senses.d: Up to the time or degree that; until.
Up to; indicates a motion towards a thing and then stopping at it.
ex: Sir Gawain rode unto the nearby castle.
And the Lord said unto Moses […]

[…] And, doubtless, unto thee is given
⁠A life that bears immortal fruit
⁠In such great offices as suit
The full-grown energies of heaven.

senses.d: Down to the last; encompassing even every.

phr: do unto others as you would have them do unto you
sufficient unto the day is the evil thereof
